---
title: Add transaction history
description: "Predict a dispute for every transaction in an account's history using shared context."
engine: markdown
---

The [first model](your-first-model.qmd) uses a dataset with one payment per
row. Suppose you can also supply the earlier transactions for each payment's
account. Prepare a new dataset with one account-review observation per row:
the latest payment appears once, at the end of a `trxns` list containing that
history. Each listed transaction has its own dispute target.

The business question becomes more specific: which transactions in the account
will receive a dispute report after review? Visits to the same merchant, changes in
amount, and booking-time patterns can provide context. An **event
history** preserves those observations so the model can learn their
relationships. Compare it with your existing aggregate features to find out
whether that detail improves dispute prediction.

The latest payment appears once, at the end of the same list as the earlier
events. Its amount and merchant need no separate root fields.

## Add a collection to each record

In this illustrative training row, `trxns` is oldest to newest and ends at
the payment being assessed. Each item keeps its booking time, amount, and
merchant together. The common review cutoff is immediately after the final
booking on May 28; every `disputed` label records whether a new dispute was
reported against that transaction in the following 30 days. These labels are
attached after the window closes:

```yaml
payment_id: payment-42
trxns:
  - transaction_id: trxn-40
    booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    disputed: false
  - transaction_id: trxn-41
    booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: true
  - transaction_id: trxn-42
    booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
    disputed: false
```

The whole sequence is known at that cutoff, so it is valid context for
every prediction. [Prepare observations](prepare-observations.qmd)
defines the cutoff, the label window, and the ordering rules in full.

The whole record above is **one observation and one Parquet row**. Its three
transactions are items inside that observation. Another row describes another
account review and can contain a different number of transactions.

`payment_id` identifies the review decision; `transaction_id` identifies an
item inside its history. Keep them in the data for matching results later.
They are application metadata and are not declared as model inputs here.

List order says which transaction came first. `booked_at` supplies calendar
parts that can reveal recurring patterns, not the elapsed time between
transactions.

A fixed feature table might retain total spend and transaction count. Here,
the amount and merchant stay paired within each event: a cafe payment and a
visit to North Market remain distinguishable. This gives the model evidence
for learning account behavior without deciding every summary in advance.

## Describe the collection with a branch

Build a new model for these history-shaped records. This construction starts
with fresh weights; it does not modify or transfer learning from the flat model.

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

`Branch` describes a collection of records with the same fields. This branch
keeps at most 32 transactions; `overflow="tail"` retains the last 32, including
the latest payment. `mask=True` hides every transaction's dispute label and
trains the model to predict it from the shared context.

Each field definition and its learned weights are reused at every transaction
position. You declare `amount` once, and it reads every retained transaction's
amount. `length=32` limits items inside each observation; it does not set the
number of observations in a training batch.

The collection remains variable-length: one account can supply three
transactions and another twenty. The declared branch generates the model's
history structure, and training learns how its fields contribute context.
The later [nested-context example](nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd)
places collections inside transactions and adds another history alongside them.

## Use the same training steps

Train this new model with the history present in each record. Your application
supplies Parquet files with the nested structure shown above:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=20)
```

`batch_size=128` now counts account-review observations, each with up to 32
transactions. The `payments/history/` files have a different row structure
from the first tutorial's `payments/flat/` files. Keep the two datasets and
their models distinct.

Prediction files keep the same transaction list and omit `disputed` from each
record:

```python
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/history/requests.parquet",
)
predictions = model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

`predictions.trxns` holds one result per retained transaction;
[Read predictions](read-predictions.qmd) shows how to extract each
probability.
